claims.text: Formation of coherent nanoscale domains is the primary determinant of wear performance in HEA protective coatings.
Coherent ordered precipitates or nanoclusters obstruct dislocation motion.
Coherent nanoscale domains mitigate abrasive wear by increasing hardness.
Coherent nanoscale domains increase resistance to crack propagation.
Changing heat-treatment temperature can selectively promote or suppress coherent nanoscale-domain formation in the coating.
An optimized heat treatment will produce more coherent nanoscale domains than the as-deposited or suboptimally treated baseline.
The relevant structural mediator is the volume fraction and size of coherent precipitates or nanoclusters in the HEA matrix.
Coherent precipitates inhibit crack initiation at interfaces.
Impeded dislocation motion and inhibited crack initiation improve coating hardness and wear resistance.
Samples with a higher density of coherent nanoscale domains will have lower wear rates than baseline samples with fewer or no such domains.
Samples with a higher density of coherent nanoscale domains will have higher hardness than baseline samples.
The treated and baseline groups will differ significantly in hardness and wear rate.
The hypothesis is expected to apply to HEA coatings capable of forming coherent domains under conventional heat treatments of approximately 700–1000 °C.
The hypothesis may not apply to compositions that preclude formation of the proposed precipitates.
The hypothesis may not apply when environmental temperature exceeds the thermal-stability limit of the precipitate phase.
The optimal size and volume fraction of coherent nanoscale domains are not established.
Different HEA compositions may exhibit different precipitation behavior.
